quiz: Think about inversions: which simple sort does less work when only a few pairs are out of order?
Count the pairs that are in the wrong order. Each adjacent swap fixes exactly one such pair.
Look at how small the range of possible values is. Can you use the value itself as an index?
Sort 21, 25, 23 by ones digit, then by tens digit with an unstable pass. What can happen to numbers that share the tens digit?
Count the levels of splitting and the work done on each level. Merging two arrays also needs somewhere to put the result.
When a right item is taken, count how many left items are still waiting and bigger than it.
On sorted input, the last element is always the largest. How many items does each partition remove?
Only one side is explored, and on average it shrinks by half. Add up N plus N/2 plus N/4 and so on.
Check for integer overflow with subtraction, and check that the result can be negative, zero and positive.
An algorithm that swaps items far apart can jump an equal item over another. Check each algorithm for that.
The intervals overlap if the current start is not past the last end. The new end is the larger of the two ends.

Treat meetings as half-open: a meeting ending at 5 frees its room for one starting at 5. Find the maximum overlap.

interview: Give the time, space and stability of each, then name real uses such as small or nearly sorted inputs and few-swaps cases.
Explain the decision tree lower bound for comparison sorts, then how counting and radix sort use values as indexes, with their costs.
Describe split, recursive sort and two-pointer merge, then solve the recurrence by counting levels and work per level.
Split inversions into left, right and cross pairs, and explain how merging counts cross pairs when a right item is taken.
Describe how each scheme moves its pointers and where the pivot ends up, and compare swaps and behaviour on equal values.
Name the bad pivot cases and the stack depth, then defences like random pivots, median of three and introsort fallback.
Compare time, memory and when each fits: sorting is simplest, a size k heap suits streams, quickselect is fastest on average.
Explain what negative, zero and positive mean, multi-key comparisons, and bugs like subtraction overflow and broken contracts.
Define stability and give cases where it matters, such as multi-pass sorting of records and radix sort.
Cover sorting by start, the sweep that extends with max, why it is correct, and pitfalls like touching ends and in-place sorting.
Describe the three-phase walk for one insert, then a sorted tree structure keyed by start for many inserts.
Explain that rooms equal the maximum overlap, then cover the heap of end times and the sorted start and end sweep.
Contrast what is used for primitive arrays and for objects, and explain why stability matters only for objects.
Talk about reading clues in the problem, such as pairs with a condition, top k, small value range, or start and end ranges.
